title: Indexes
subtitle: Accelerate reads with ordered access paths while accounting for write and storage cost
objectives: Explain what an index is and why it turns a scan into ~20 steps
Describe why databases use B-trees, and what sortedness buys you
Account for the real cost of an index: writes, disk, and when the planner ignores it
Design a composite index for a real query — right columns, right order — and verify with `EXPLAIN`

exercises.title: A B-tree index maps ordered key values to row locations
exercises.body: A common B-tree index stores ordered values from one or more columns with row locations. A lookup traverses the tree and follows matching locations. Hash, inverted, and spatial indexes organize keys differently for other query patterns.
exercises.note: Because an index is derived from the table, affected `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` operations must also maintain its entries.

exercises.prompt: A tenant dashboard filters by `tenant_id` and sorts by `created_at`. Replace two separate indexes with one composite index in query order.
exercises.beforeStatus: QUERY WORK · filter many tenant rows, then sort them
exercises.afterStatus: QUERY WORK · seek to one tenant's ordered range and read the first page
exercises.result: Filtering and ordering now use one index walk
exercises.why: With equality on `tenant_id` followed by ordering on `created_at`, the composite index stores each tenant's rows together in time order. Reversing the columns would not provide the same efficient tenant-specific range.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A tenant dashboard filters by `tenant_id` and sorts by `created_at`. Replace two separate indexes with one composite index in query order. Place Composite index, First page. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Dashboard query → Composite index; Composite index → First page. That topology is the evidence for the answer: With equality on `tenant_id` followed by ordering on `created_at`, the composite index stores each tenant's rows together in time order. Reversing the columns would not provide the same efficient tenant-specific range.

exercises.prompt: A 1,000-page book. You want every page mentioning 'sharding.' You could read all 1,000 pages — or flip to the index at the back. What does that index give you?
choices: A sorted list of terms, each with page numbers — so you jump straight there
A faster way to read every page
Nothing you couldn't get by reading
exercises.why: The book index is a separate sorted mapping from each term to the pages containing it. Sorting supports a fast term lookup, and the stored page numbers direct the reader to the relevant pages. The work then scales with locating the term and visiting its matches.

exercises.prompt: So what IS a database index?
choices: A faster copy of the whole table
A derived access structure that organizes keys for supported query patterns
A cache of recent query results
A compressed version of the table
exercises.why: A database index is a derived access structure maintained as table rows change. A B-tree orders keys, a hash index groups hash values, and inverted or spatial indexes organize different lookup relationships; sortedness is one mechanism, not the definition of every index.

exercises.prompt: A B-tree page can choose among roughly 400 child pages. Reaching one key among 1 million entries takes about 3 page levels instead of scanning up to 1 million rows. What follows?
choices: Both approaches scale the same because they search the same table
The index sharply reduces lookup work when the predicate matches its key
The index removes all storage reads
The scan becomes faster as the table grows
exercises.why: With fan-out near 400, three B-tree levels can address tens of millions of key positions, so a matching predicate eliminates most ranges with each page read. The engine may still fetch the table row after reaching the leaf; the example describes page levels, not binary-tree comparisons.

exercises.prompt: With fan-out near 400, growing from 1 million to 1 billion entries adds roughly one B-tree page level: about 3 to about 4. What does that show?
choices: Balanced-index lookup work grows much more slowly than the row count
Every index lookup always takes exactly 4 page reads
A billion-row table occupies only 50% more storage
A full scan also grows from 3 to 4 checks
exercises.why: The table grows by a factor of 1,000 while the approximate B-tree height grows by one page level because each internal page chooses among hundreds of children. Exact height depends on page size and key width; the point is high fan-out and logarithmic growth, not a 20-step binary tree.

exercises.prompt: Without a useful index, the database performs a full table ______; with one, it jumps straight to the rows.
exercises.why: A full table scan reads rows and evaluates the predicate against each one. The planner uses this path when no usable index exists or when an index would cost more than sequentially scanning the table.

exercises.prompt: An index is derived data — everything in it also exists in the table. What follows from that?
choices: You can drop and rebuild an index without losing any data
Dropping an index deletes the underlying rows
The index is the source of truth
Indexes must be backed up separately or data is lost
exercises.why: An ordinary index is derived from table columns, so the database can reconstruct it by scanning the table. Dropping it removes the access path, not the rows. An index that backs a `UNIQUE` constraint also enforces an invariant, so the database may require the constraint to be removed before that index can be dropped.

exercises.title: A B-tree packs many sorted keys into each storage page
exercises.body: Each internal B-tree node contains many separator keys and pointers to child pages. One page read therefore chooses among hundreds of subtrees. A leaf page stores ordered index keys and row locations. High fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so a lookup reaches a leaf with only a few page reads.
exercises.note: Range queries seek to the first matching leaf entry once, then scan adjacent ordered entries for the remaining rows.

exercises.prompt: A query filters `tenant_id = 42` and sorts by newest `created_at`, but the index contains only `created_at`. Match the index order to the query.
choices: Use separate indexes on each column
choiceFeedback: Starting with the timestamp range mixes entries from every tenant before the tenant filter can narrow them.
The optimizer may combine indexes, but that does not directly provide one tenant's rows in timestamp order.
The equality prefix isolates the tenant, then the second column supplies timestamp order.
exercises.beforeStatus: QUERY · scans timestamps across every tenant
exercises.afterStatus: QUERY · seeks tenant 42 · reads newest matching entries
exercises.result: The index prefix now matches the equality filter before the range order
exercises.why: Putting the equality column first groups one tenant's entries together; `created_at` then preserves the required order inside that group. Reversing the columns cannot efficiently isolate one tenant after starting a broad timestamp range.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A query filters `tenant_id = 42` and sorts by newest `created_at`, but the index contains only `created_at`. Match the index order to the query. Place Tenant 42 query, INDEX(tenant_id, created_at). Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Tenant 42 query → INDEX(tenant_id, created_at). That topology is the evidence for the answer: Putting the equality column first groups one tenant's entries together; `created_at` then preserves the required order inside that group. Reversing the columns cannot efficiently isolate one tenant after starting a broad timestamp range.

exercises.prompt: Databases use B-trees for indexes rather than simple binary trees. Why?
choices: A B-tree node holds hundreds of keys, matching how disks read in big blocks — so one disk read gets you hundreds of keys instead of one
exercises.why: A B-tree node is sized to hold many keys in one storage page. Each page read can therefore choose among hundreds of child ranges, producing a wide, shallow tree and reducing random page reads compared with a binary tree that branches only twice per node.

exercises.prompt: Build a non-covering B-tree lookup for `WHERE email = 'x@y.com'`. The executor narrows through internal pages, finds a locator at the leaf, then fetches the full row.
exercises.why: The executor follows separator keys through internal B-tree pages, finds the email and row locator in a leaf, then fetches the table row because the index does not cover every requested column. If no suitable index exists, the database may scan the full table, making lookup work and latency grow with row count.

exercises.prompt: Why can an index on `created_at` efficiently answer 'all rows from last week'?
choices: It can't — indexes only do exact matches
Because the index is SORTED: once you find the start of the range, the rest sit right next to each other
exercises.why: Because `created_at` keys are ordered, the engine navigates to the first key in last week's range and scans adjacent index entries until the range ends. A hash index discards key order, so it can support equality but cannot traverse a date interval in order.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to what it gives you.

pairs.right: Read every row and check it

exercises.why: A B-tree preserves key order, supporting equality, ranges, and ordered traversal. A hash index maps a complete key to a bucket for equality lookup but provides no useful ordering. A full scan checks every row, while an index lookup follows the chosen access structure.

exercises.prompt: Your query ends with `ORDER BY created_at`, and there's an index on `created_at`. What's the bonus?
choices: The index is already in sorted order, so the database can skip the sort step entirely
The rows come back in random order
exercises.why: A compatible B-tree scan emits entries in `created_at` order, so the executor can satisfy `ORDER BY created_at` without a separate sort. This matters when the result would exceed sort memory, because an external sort writes and merges temporary runs on storage.

exercises.prompt: What makes an index useful for a particular query?
choices: Its access structure can prune most candidates for that query instead of checking every row
exercises.why: An index is useful when its organization matches the query and eliminates most candidates: B-trees use ordered ranges, hash indexes use buckets, and inverted indexes map terms to documents. No one property such as sortedness explains every index family.

exercises.title: Each index adds maintenance work to table writes
exercises.body: An `INSERT` adds an entry to every applicable index. A `DELETE` removes entries, and an `UPDATE` changes each index whose key or row locator changed. For a B-tree, maintenance may dirty several pages and split a full page while preserving key order.
exercises.note: On a write-heavy table, index maintenance can become the throughput bottleneck even while the indexed reads remain fast.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Each index adds maintenance work to table writes
exercises.why: An `INSERT` adds an entry to every applicable index. A `DELETE` removes entries, and an `UPDATE` changes each index whose key or row locator changed. For a B-tree, maintenance may dirty several pages and split a full page while preserving key order. On a write-heavy table, index maintenance can become the throughput bottleneck even while the indexed reads remain fast.

exercises.prompt: You add 5 indexes to a table, then `INSERT` one row containing entries for all five. What happens?
choices: The `INSERT` must add an entry to all 5 indexes, increasing write work
exercises.why: This `INSERT` creates one entry in each of the five applicable indexes, adding page changes and log records. An `UPDATE` affects only indexes whose key or row locator changes, and some engines can avoid extra index maintenance for eligible updates.

exercises.prompt: What does each additional index cost you? Select all.
choices: More memory — indexes compete for cache
Slower reads on the indexed column
exercises.why: Every index consumes disk, adds maintenance work to affected writes, and competes with table pages and other indexes for buffer-cache memory. Reads that match the index may improve; unrelated reads can degrade if unused index pages displace hotter data.

exercises.prompt: A team adds an index on every column, 'just in case.' Result?
choices: Writes slow down, disk use grows, and many workload-irrelevant indexes receive maintenance without helping the measured queries
exercises.why: An index on every column adds write maintenance, disk use, and cache pressure even when no query uses most of those access paths. Additional candidates can also complicate planning. Index-usage statistics and representative query plans are needed before safely removing an index.

exercises.prompt: You have an index on `country`. For `WHERE country = 'US'`, where 90% of rows are US, the planner does a full scan anyway. Why?
choices: It's a bug in the planner
Reading 90% of the table via an index means randomly jumping to nearly every row — streaming the whole table sequentially is genuinely faster
Indexes don't work on text columns
exercises.why: The predicate's estimated matching fraction is 90%, so the index would return nearly one locator per table row. Following those locators can cause many random table-page accesses; a sequential scan reads each table page once and is often cheaper. In common optimizer terminology, 90% matching is poorly selective.

exercises.prompt: Which is cheaper to use as an indexed primary key: an auto-incrementing id, or a random UUID?
choices: The increasing id usually inserts near the B-tree's right edge, while random UUIDs scatter inserts across many pages
The random UUID — randomness spreads load evenly
exercises.why: Increasing identifiers usually insert near the right edge of a B-tree, preserving locality and making page behavior predictable. Random universally unique identifiers (UUIDs) insert throughout the tree, increasing cache misses, page splits, and index fragmentation; time-ordered UUID schemes can recover locality while retaining distributed generation.

exercises.prompt: A write-heavy audit log: billions of appends, queried only during rare investigations. Slide toward how many indexes you'd add.
exercises.why: Every audit append pays the maintenance cost of each index, while rare investigations collect the read benefit infrequently. Keeping only indexes required for ingestion or common operational queries protects write throughput; occasional scans can be accepted or run on an analytical copy.

exercises.title: The query planner uses an index when its estimated cost is lower
exercises.body: For each plan, the database estimates how many rows a predicate will match and the I/O needed to fetch them. An index is effective when it narrows the result to a small fraction of the table. If most rows match, many pointer-driven row fetches can cost more than one sequential table scan.
exercises.note: Skewed or stale statistics can produce a bad row-count estimate, causing the planner to choose an index scan or table scan with the higher actual cost.

exercises.prompt: You index a boolean `is_active` column where 95% of rows are true. Does it help `WHERE is_active = true`?
choices: Barely — it matches 95% of rows, so it isn't selective, and the planner will likely scan anyway
exercises.why: `is_active = true` returns 95% of the table, so an index lookup would visit almost every row and usually costs more than one sequential scan. `is_active = false` selects 5% of the rows, where targeted index access can be cheaper. A partial index containing only inactive rows further reduces index size and write-maintenance cost for that query.

exercises.prompt: Assume a conventional B-tree plan with skip scan disabled. Which query can efficiently bound a contiguous range in `(last_name, first_name)`?
exercises.why: The B-tree is ordered by `last_name`, then `first_name`, so `last_name = 'Lovelace'` bounds one contiguous range. With skip scan disabled, `first_name` alone cannot directly bound one range, though an engine may still scan the index or use skip scan when its cost model and data distribution favor it.

exercises.prompt: With a conventional B-tree range scan and skip scan disabled, which predicates can directly bound a contiguous range in `(a, b, c)`? Select all.
exercises.why: The index is ordered by `a`, then `b`, then `c`, so the stated conventional scan directly bounds ranges from the leftmost prefixes `(a)`, `(a,b)`, and `(a,b,c)`. Later columns can still filter or cover a query, and engines that support skip scan may exploit `b` alone under favorable distributions.

exercises.prompt: Query: `SELECT email FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com'`, with an index on `email`. Why might the database answer this without reading the table at all?
choices: Because the index already contains every column the query asks for
It can't — it always has to read the row
exercises.why: The predicate and result both require only `email`, which is present in the index. This permits an index-only scan that avoids fetching the full row when the engine can establish row visibility from index-related metadata; otherwise it may still consult the table.

exercises.prompt: How do you find out whether your query is actually using an index?
choices: Run `EXPLAIN` — the database shows you the plan it chose
exercises.why: `EXPLAIN` reports the optimizer's chosen operators, such as a sequential scan or index scan, along with estimated rows and costs. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` also executes the query and reports actual timing and row counts, which helps detect estimation errors.

exercises.prompt: A query filters `WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'open'`, then sorts `ORDER BY created_at`. Which single composite index best serves it?
exercises.why: With `(user_id, status, created_at)`, the two equality predicates identify one contiguous index range, and entries inside it are already ordered by `created_at`. Starting with `created_at` would interleave many users and statuses across the requested time order, preventing the same direct narrowing.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest one-sentence summary of indexing?
choices: Index every column so every query is fast
An index is a derived access structure that trades write work and disk for supported reads — design it for real queries and verify with `EXPLAIN`
Avoid indexes; they slow down writes
Let the database figure it out automatically
exercises.why: An index is derived data maintained on each affected write, so it trades write throughput, storage, and cache space for faster matching reads. Useful indexes align with real predicates and ordering, exclude enough rows to justify lookup, and are verified in the chosen plan with `EXPLAIN`.

exercises.prompt: A marketplace query filters by `seller_id`, then returns that seller's newest listings by `created_at`. Which index most directly supports the access path?
choices: One separate index on every column
exercises.why: Equality on the leading seller key narrows one seller's range, and the second key already orders that range by creation time. Reversing the columns groups all sellers by time first.
